scenes.say: In 1815, a single mountain exploded. Within a year, it had changed the weather of the entire planet.
It brought snow in the middle of summer. It starved people on the other side of the world.
And strangely, it also gave us Frankenstein, the modern vampire, and maybe even the bicycle.
This is the story of the year without a summer.
The mountain was called Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa, in what is now Indonesia.
It stood about four thousand three hundred meters tall, and it had been quiet for centuries.
On the evening of April fifth, 1815, it woke up, with a blast heard hundreds of miles away.
Soldiers far across the sea thought they were hearing cannon fire, and marched out to look for a battle.
But that was only the warning. Five days later, on April tenth, the real eruption began.
Witnesses saw three columns of fire rise into the sky, until the whole mountain looked like flowing, glowing rock.
It was the most powerful eruption in recorded history. The explosions were heard more than two thousand kilometers away.
The mountain blew out so much rock and ash that it lost about a third of its height.
Ash buried whole villages. Giant waves hit the coast. For days, the sky stayed as black as night.
At least ten thousand people died in the eruption itself. Famine and disease on the nearby islands killed tens of thousands more.
The local language of Tambora vanished with its people. A whole culture was wiped out in a single week.
But the disaster did not stay in Indonesia. Tambora had thrown a huge cloud of gas high above the weather.
Up there, it became a thin mist that spread around the whole world, like a veil across the sun.
It bounced sunlight back into space. Slowly, the planet began to cool.
The drop was less than one degree on average. That does not sound like much. It was enough.
In 1816, summer simply failed to arrive across much of Europe and North America.
In New England, snow fell in June. Frost came in July, and again in August.
Farmers watched their crops freeze in the fields. People later called it, eighteen hundred and froze to death.
In Europe, it rained almost without stopping. Harvests rotted, and the price of bread climbed higher and higher.
scenes.label: BREAD

scenes.say: Hungry crowds rioted in Britain and France. In Switzerland, the famine was so bad that the government declared a national emergency.
Reports from Switzerland describe desperate families eating moss.
In China, cold and floods ruined the rice harvest in Yunnan, bringing years of hunger.
One historian later called it the last great hunger crisis of the Western world.
In America, thousands of farming families gave up and headed west, looking for kinder weather.
And beside a lake in Switzerland, the terrible weather trapped a group of young writers indoors.
Among them were the poet Lord Byron, his doctor John Polidori, the poet Percy Shelley, and eighteen year old Mary Godwin.
Mary was the youngest in the room. She was about to write one of the most famous books in history.
Bored, with rain hammering the windows, Byron set a challenge. Each of them would write a ghost story.
Mary struggled for days. Then, one night, she imagined a scientist who brings a dead body to life.
She turned it into a novel. In 1818, it was published as Frankenstein, often called the first science fiction story.
scenes.title: FRANKEN STEIN

scenes.say: Polidori wrote a tale too. He called it The Vampyre, about a charming nobleman who drinks blood.
It shaped almost every vampire story that followed, including Dracula, nearly eighty years later.
scenes.title: DRACULA

scenes.say: And Byron wrote a poem called Darkness, about a world where the sun has gone out.
The ash even changed art. For years, sunsets glowed deep red and orange, and painters put those skies on canvas.
The painter Turner became famous for skies that seemed to be on fire.
And then there is the bicycle. With oats so expensive, feeding a horse became a luxury.
scenes.label: OATS

scenes.say: In 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais revealed his running machine. Two wheels, a wooden frame, and no horse required.
On its first big ride, it covered about thirteen kilometers in roughly an hour, faster than the mail coach.
Some historians think the hungry years pushed him to invent it. It was the ancestor of every bicycle on Earth.
Here is the strangest part. At the time, nobody knew why any of this was happening.
People blamed sunspots. Some blamed God. A few even blamed lightning rods.
It took about a century for scientists to connect the frozen summer to a mountain on the far side of the world.
The proof was hiding in the ice. Ancient snow in Greenland and Antarctica still holds the sulfur from 1815.
Today, Tambora is quiet again. Where its peak once stood, there is a crater about six kilometers wide.
And it could happen again. Eruptions this big seem to come once or twice every thousand years.
scenes.sub: once or twice per thousand years

scenes.say: One mountain. One week in April. And the world got famine, a monster, a vampire, and a bicycle.
History is stranger than anything we could make up.
